clue.text: Though sweet this fool may be, lovers find one de trop

definitions.text: Though sweet this fool may be
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fruit that is made into a fool, a creamy pudding, even though the fruit itself is sour
second meaning: an unwanted third person tagging along with a courting couple

explanation.surface: A sweet-natured fool is still in the way when two lovers want to be alone.
explanation.walkthrough: A fool here is a British dessert of puréed fruit and cream; 'de trop' is French for superfluous, unwanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit is famously sour, and 'playing gooseberry' is the British idiom for being the unwanted chaperone of a couple.

clue.text: State limits of patience, making us yawn

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia

indicators.note: the limits of a word are its two boundaries, its first and last letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone stretched to the end of their patience makes everyone yawn.
explanation.definitionFit: To yawn and to open the mouth wide are the same action, and a chasm can also be said to yawn or gape.

clue.text: Has topless dresses

indicators.note: topless means without the top, which in a down answer is the first letter

parts.note: gowns are dresses

explanation.surface: Owns some topless dresses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless dresses' tempts as a fashion phrase, but topless acts on the word dresses.
explanation.definitionFit: To have something and to possess it as one's property are synonyms, both third-person singular verbs here.

clue.text: Constable holds one up in the issue "Freedom from Bondage"

indicators.note: holds says one piece grips another inside it

parts.note: an emanation is something issued or given out

indicators.note: in a down answer, up means reading the letters from bottom to top, backwards
in places the preceding letters inside the following word

parts.note: PC is police constable
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A policeman holds up a copy of a magazine with the headline about release from slavery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' reverses only in a down entry; the small container is built first, flipped, then put inside the larger word.
explanation.definitionFit: Emancipation is release from slavery or restriction, which is exactly liberation from bondage.

clue.text: Result level on the end of it

parts.note: level means even

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: The outcome was a draw, level at the finish.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun can mean an outcome or consequence, as in 'in the event' meaning as things turned out.

clue.text: Chaser, or 'e could be a runner of course

indicators.note: could be says the letters before it might form something else once rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
Cockney he with its H dropped, leaving just the one letter

explanation.surface: A steeplechaser, or he, might be running on the course.
explanation.walkthrough: A chaser is a steeplechase horse, so the surface already points at the answer; the apostrophe drops the H from 'he'.
explanation.definitionFit: A runner on a racecourse is a horse entered in a race, with a pun on 'of course' as 'on the course'.

clue.text: Adventure film in the picture-theatre

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the words that follow, spanning a word break

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second; the rest is cover

explanation.surface: A big adventure movie showing at the local cinema.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters straddle 'thE PICture'; picture-theatre is an old word for a cinema, which helps the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand, sweeping film of heroic adventure on a large scale is called by this noun, borrowed from long heroic poems.

clue.text: Tyler's followers accepting money? Just a joke!

indicators.note: accepting means taking something in, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: Wat Tyler led the Peasants' Revolt of 1381
L is the pound sign, standing for money

explanation.surface: Rebels taking bribes? Surely you jest.
explanation.walkthrough: L goes into PEASANTRY after its first letter. L for pound comes from the Latin libra.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleasantry is a light jocular remark, a bit of banter, so it is merely a joke.

clue.text: Treat for kids by Church youth leaders on site of Eliot's Mill

indicators.note: leaders are the front runners, so each of the two preceding words gives its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word
by in the sense of along with, in addition to
the first letter of the word
George Eliot wrote The Mill on the Floss, the Floss being a river

explanation.surface: A church youth group hands out sweets beside a famous mill.
explanation.walkthrough: George Eliot's novel The Mill on the Floss names the river; the 'on' of the title is mirrored by the link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Spun sugar on a stick, sold at fairs, is a sweet treat chiefly enjoyed by children; Americans call it cotton candy.

clue.text: Joshua's after these books

parts.note: surface reading: someone called Joshua is hunting for some books
setter's reading: the Book of Joshua comes after the first five books of the Bible

explanation.walkthrough: 'After' means chasing in the surface, but in the cryptic sense it is order in the Old Testament: Joshua is the sixth book.
explanation.definitionFit: This Greek-derived name covers Genesis through Deuteronomy, the five books of Moses that precede the Book of Joshua in the Bible.

clue.text: Put this Scottish infant on the bottle

definitions.text: Put this Scottish infant on the bottle
definitions.note: a verb phrase: to move a baby off the breast
definitions.meaning: first meaning: to move a baby from breast milk to other feeding, such as the bottle
second meaning: the Scots word for a small child

explanation.walkthrough: In Scotland a child is a 'wean'; the same word, as an English verb, means to stop breastfeeding, often by moving to bottles.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scots noun for a young child doubles as the ordinary verb for weaning a baby from the breast onto other feeding.

clue.text: Electrical fault located, it's said, showing lack of providence

indicators.note: it's said tells us to go by how the preceding words are spoken

parts.note: a short is an electrical fault, and located means sited

explanation.surface: An electrician finds a fault but has failed to plan ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: A short circuit is the fault; sited and sighted sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally unable to see far, figuratively it describes failing to plan for the future, which is lacking providence or foresight.

clue.text: Drink tax of old which needs revision — heavens!

parts.note: a scot was a medieval tax, as in scot-free

indicators.note: something needing revision has to be reworked, so the word before it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the sky is the heavens

explanation.surface: An old tax on drink that badly needs revising, for heaven's sake.
explanation.walkthrough: Scot is an old word for a tax or levy, surviving in 'scot-free'.
explanation.definitionFit: The spirit distilled in Scotland is a drink, so the general word stands for this specific example of it.

clue.text: Old man's '5 bottle makes me so healthy in retrospect

parts.note: surface padding: a nod to the Biblical patriarch the bottle is named after; the printed word here is garbled in the scan
taken as written
so means thus

indicators.note: in retrospect means looking back, so the word just before it is read backwards

parts.note: hale means healthy

explanation.surface: An old man boasts that his bottle keeps him so healthy, looking back.
explanation.walkthrough: The Biblical patriarch who lived 969 years gives his name to the bottle, so the old man is a second hint to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A very large champagne bottle holding eight standard bottles is named after the oldest man in the Bible.

clue.text: Very bad, getting rope all tangled with bed

indicators.note: something tangled is twisted out of order, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A terrible state: a rope knotted up with the bedclothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Deplorable means deserving strong condemnation, shockingly bad, an intensified synonym for awful.

clue.text: Reveille should be somewhat surprising

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a bugle call at dawn that opens sleepers' eyes, taken literally
second meaning: something astonishing or revealing, read as 'some-what surprising'

explanation.surface: The morning bugle call ought to come as a bit of a shock.
explanation.walkthrough: Reveille is the military wake-up call; 'somewhat' is read as 'some thing that is', a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a thing that wakes you, the compound is also the idiom for a revelation or startling discovery.

clue.text: It makes one forget being imprisoned in Sheen perhaps

indicators.note: in places the preceding letters inside the following word
perhaps says the word before it is only one possible arrangement of its letters

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
pent, as in pent-up, means shut in

explanation.surface: Something that makes you forget being locked up in Sheen, a place in south-west London.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheen looks like the London district, but it is just letters to shuffle around PENT.
explanation.definitionFit: In Homer's Odyssey this drug banishes grief and memory; it is also the genus of pitcher plants.

clue.text: Learn disorder of the kidneys

indicators.note: a disorder throws things out of their proper arrangement, so the word before it is jumbled

parts.note: the five letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Study up on a kidney disease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disorder of the kidneys' reads as a medical condition, but disorder is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: This adjective, from Latin ren for kidney, describes anything relating to those organs, such as a renal artery.

clue.text: Explosive destiny for a serf

parts.note: HE is the standard abbreviation for high explosive
one's lot is one's fate

explanation.surface: A fiery fate awaits a peasant.
explanation.definitionFit: The bonded labourers of ancient Sparta were a class of state serfs, and the word extends to any serf.

clue.text: Fourth estate contains certain compelling forces

indicators.note: contains says one word holds the other inside it

parts.note: the fourth estate is the press, the newspapers
certain means sure

explanation.surface: Newspapers include some powerful influences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fourth estate' is the traditional name for journalism, after the three estates of clergy, nobility and commons.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural noun for coercive influences or forces that push someone to act, matching compelling forces in number.

clue.text: We hear you are right in depth measurements in the environment

indicators.note: in places the preceding letters inside the following word

parts.note: soundings are measurements of water depth

indicators.note: we hear says to take the next words by their sound

parts.note: said aloud, the two words are the letters U and R, as in text-speak
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Depth soundings, we're told, are correct in their setting.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'you are' is taken by sound, as in text-speak; the rest is ordinary wordplay, with soundings meaning plumbed depths of water.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural noun for the conditions and place around someone, the setting one lives in, which is what environment means.

clue.text: She could become Queen of France

indicators.note: could become says the letters may be turned into something else by rearranging them

parts.note: reine is the French word for queen

explanation.surface: A woman who might one day be crowned Queen of France.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder is not in the clue's English words but their French translation.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name, of Greek origin meaning peace, so any woman bearing it can be referred to as she.

clue.text: The Bull seen outside a pub?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Taurus, one of the twelve divisions of the zodiac
second meaning: the painted board hanging outside an inn

explanation.walkthrough: The Bull is also a common British pub name, so the surface tempts one to think of an inn, but it is the zodiac.
explanation.definitionFit: Taurus is one of the astrological star signs, and every traditional British pub hangs a painted board showing its name.

clue.text: Not pleasing this sort of customer

definitions.meaning: first meaning: unattractive to look at
second meaning: from the idiom for a dangerous, aggressive person

explanation.walkthrough: 'Customer' here is the informal British use meaning a person, as in 'an awkward customer'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means unattractive or unpleasant, and 'an ugly customer' is the idiom for a threatening, nasty individual.

clue.text: See, live, part of the loan Antony requested

definitions.text: part of the loan Antony requested

parts.note: lo is an archaic exclamation meaning look, see
to be is to exist, to live

explanation.surface: Look here, live a little, take a slice of the loan Antony asked for.
explanation.walkthrough: In Julius Caesar, Mark Antony opens his speech with 'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears'.
explanation.definitionFit: Antony asked the crowd to lend him their ears, and the fleshy lower portion of an ear is a piece of one.

clue.text: It's very little to manage on, and it's usually tied up

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a tiny budget, as in running something on very little money
second meaning: a lace for fastening footwear, knotted in a bow

explanation.surface: A meagre budget, and the money's mostly tied up anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tied up' suggests money locked away in investments, but it is literal: a lace is tied.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'on a shoestring' means with a tiny budget, and literally it is a bootlace one knots.

clue.text: Good dog comes to this dirty one

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an obedient dog comes to its owner's side on command
second meaning: a cad, someone who behaves dishonourably

explanation.surface: A well-trained dog obeys commands, even a dirty one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dirty one' looks like it describes the dog or a command, but it is a separate meaning: a scoundrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogs are trained to walk at the owner's heel, and the same word is slang for a contemptible, untrustworthy man.

clue.text: 100, say, can end badly under such domination

indicators.note: badly says the preceding letters are put together wrongly, in a jumbled order

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for 100
taken as written, to join the jumble

explanation.surface: A hundred people, say, can come to grief under such tyranny.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascendancy is a position of dominance or controlling power over others, the state of being in command.
